transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, nice to meet you too, Dr. Smith. I, uh, I guess the main thing that brings me in today is... well, it’s kind of hard to explain, but I just have this constant feeling like I’ve got a motor humming right under my skin. And it really only happens—or, well, it really only becomes a problem, I guess—whenever I’m supposed to just sit still. 

You see, I work as a building cleaner, a janitor, so most of the day I'm on my feet, sweeping, buffing floors, moving from the lobby up to the third floor, which is honestly great for me. I like being on the move. But then we have these mandatory staff meetings, or, you know, on weekends I help out at my parish and we have these church event briefings that can drag on for an hour or more. And I just... I can't do it. I sit there and that motor just starts revving, and I end up shifting in my seat, crossing and uncrossing my legs, and eventually I just have to stand up. I’ll go stand in the back of the room, or I'll find some excuse to move around, like pretending I need to check the thermostat or empty a wastebasket that's already empty. I'll get up to get a cup of coffee I don't even want just to be walking. I just can't seem to stay planted in the chair like everyone else does, and my supervisor has started giving me these looks about it, like I'm not paying attention or I'm being disrespectful, which isn't it at all! It’s just getting exhausting trying to keep a lid on it, so I figured I really ought to come talk to somebody.

When you feel that 'motor' sensation, do you experience it as a physical, uncomfortable urge in your legs that is relieved by moving, or is it more of a mental feeling that you just can't keep your mind focused?

Well, it’s not really... I wouldn't call it an uncomfortable urge in my legs, exactly. Like, I know some folks get that creepy-crawly feeling in their calves, especially at night—my sister-in-law gets that, actually, she's always complaining about her legs keeping her awake when she's just trying to sit on the couch and watch her evening shows. But for me, it's not like a pain or a tingle in my legs, and it's not really localized just to my legs at all. It's my whole body. 

And as for the mental part, it's not really that I can't keep my mind focused on what's happening. I mean, I know exactly what they're talking about in those meetings. Just last week, Mr. Henderson was going over the new chemical storage protocols for the cleaning supplies—which, by the way, we've been doing the exact same way for five years, but suddenly it's a big deal because corporate changed the color of the labels on the industrial bleach—and I heard every single word he said. My mind wasn't wandering off into the clouds. I was paying attention. 

The problem was just that my body wanted to be *doing* the thing, not sitting in a folding chair listening to him talk about doing the thing. It’s like... if you leave a car idling too long, it just wants to be put in drive. So I don't feel an uncomfortable ache in my legs, and my mind isn't lost in space. I just feel this pressure building up, this "go, go, go" feeling. I start tapping my pen, or I start bouncing my heel—not because my leg hurts or needs relief, but just to let off some of that steam, you know? And if the meeting goes past twenty minutes, tapping the pen just isn't enough anymore. So, yeah, I guess neither of those descriptions really fits exactly what I'm feeling.
Have you ever found yourself in trouble with the law, or have you ever been told that you frequently disregard rules or the rights of others in your daily life?

No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I've never been in trouble with the law, not even close. Well, I got a speeding ticket once back in, oh, I think it was 1998? I was driving down Route 4, and you know how the speed limit drops from 55 to 35 right after the overpass, and I just didn't slow down fast enough. But that's it! I've never been arrested or anything like that. 

And as far as rules go... I actually really like rules. In my line of work, rules are what keep you safe. You don't mix ammonia and bleach, you know? That's a rule you don't mess with, or you end up with mustard gas in the mop closet. I always follow the protocols, I read the safety data sheets, I make sure the wet floor signs are out—even if the floor is barely damp, I put them out because that's the rule and you don't want someone slipping and breaking a hip. 

And about disregarding other people's rights... I try really hard to be respectful of everyone. I mean, I clean up after people all day. You have to have a certain amount of respect for folks to do that day in and day out without getting bitter. Sometimes I might interrupt someone, I guess? Like if I have a thought, it just kind of pops out before I can stop it, especially if I'm excited about something, but it's never because I don't care about what they're saying or because I think my thing is more important. It's just that the thought is moving so fast it bypasses the filter. But I always apologize right away. My wife, well, she used to get annoyed by it, but she knows I don't mean any harm. I'm definitely not out here breaking laws or stepping on people's toes on purpose. I just... I just have a hard time sitting still, that's all.
Did you experience this same need to move around or difficulty sitting still when you were a child, for instance while you were in school?

Oh, gosh, yes. Way back. I mean, it’s funny you ask about school because that was... well, that was a whole ordeal. I remember being in grade school, maybe third grade with Mrs. Gable—or no, maybe it was fourth grade with Mr. Harrison, anyway, it doesn't matter, but I was always, always getting in trouble for it. 

I just could not stay at my desk. We’d be supposed to be doing silent reading or practicing our spelling words, and I’d just pop right out of my seat. I’d wander over to the pencil sharpener even if my pencil was perfectly sharp, or I'd go look at the class hamster, or I'd just stand up by my desk for no reason. I just couldn't stay glued to the chair like the other kids. 

And it wasn't just the sitting, either. I was terrible about talking over the teacher. She’d be standing at the chalkboard, explaining what we were supposed to do for a science project or something, and I’d just start talking right over her with whatever thought popped into my head. Or I’d just grab my pencil and start rushing ahead, doing the worksheet before she even finished giving the directions. Half the time I’d do the whole page completely wrong because I didn't wait to hear the second half of the instructions, but I just couldn't wait. The waiting was like physical torture, just sitting there listening when I could be doing it. 

My mother, God rest her soul, she used to say it all the time. She’d be trying to get me to just sit down and eat my dinner without jumping up to check on the dog or look out the kitchen window, and she’d look at my dad and say I acted like I was wound too tight. That was her exact phrase, "wound too tight." Like one of those little wind-up toy cars, you know? You turn the key and it just vibrates in your hand until you put it down and it zips off across the linoleum. That’s exactly how I felt even as a little kid. So, yeah, it’s definitely not a new thing at all, it’s just that back then they just called you a nuisance and sent you to the principal's office, whereas now I'm an adult and I'm supposed to be able to sit through a staff meeting without looking like a jumping bean, but it's the exact same feeling I had when I was eight...
